explanation:
## Two kinds of borrow, and the rule between them

```rust
fn total(v: &Vec<i64>) -> i64            // shared:    read only, many allowed
fn add_to_all(v: &mut Vec<i64>, d: i64)  // exclusive: may write, one allowed
```

The compiler tracks, for every value, which references to it are alive. The rule
it enforces:

```
      &T  &T  &T      any number of shared borrows, simultaneously
  or  &mut T          exactly one exclusive borrow, and nothing else
```

`&mut` is often read as "mutable reference", and "exclusive reference" is the
better name: the thing that makes it special is not that it can write, it is
that nothing else may exist while it does.

## Why that one rule is worth so much

**It is iterator invalidation, solved.**

```rust
let first = &v[0];
v.push(99);                 // error: cannot borrow `v` as mutable
println!("{}", first);
```

`push` may reallocate the vector's buffer, which would leave `first` dangling.
This is exactly the C++ bug from the dynamic-array problem:

```cpp
int* p = &v[0];
v.push_back(4);             // may reallocate
*p = 99;                    // use-after-free, if it did
```

In C++ that compiles, and whether it breaks depends on whether the capacity
happened to be sufficient. AddressSanitizer catches it at runtime if you are
running under it and if the test exercises that path. Rust rejects it at compile
time, always, with no runtime cost.

**It is the data race, solved.** A data race needs two threads, one of them
writing, no synchronisation. The rule makes "someone else can see this while I
write" unrepresentable, so the race cannot be expressed. That is why Rust can
offer threads without a garbage collector and without a convention about who
owns what - the same borrow rules that stop the single-threaded aliasing bug
stop the concurrent one.

## The error in `push_total`, and why it is not pedantry

```rust
fn push_total(v: &mut Vec<i64>) {
    v.push(total(v));        // error[E0502]
}
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `*v` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |
  |     v.push(total(v));
  |     -------------^--
  |     |      |     |
  |     |      |     immutable borrow occurs here
  |     |      mutable borrow later used by call
  |     mutable borrow occurs here
```

`push` needs the exclusive borrow; `total(v)` needs a shared one; the arguments
are evaluated while `push`'s receiver borrow is already live. The fix is to
finish one before starting the other:

```rust
let t = total(v);        // shared borrow starts and ends on this line
v.push(t);               // now the exclusive borrow is alone
```

This is not the compiler being awkward about a harmless case. `push` can
reallocate, and `total` is walking the buffer - a hypothetical implementation
that evaluated the argument lazily, or a future version of `push` that touched
the data, would genuinely be unsafe. Rust rejects based on the *signatures*, not
on what the bodies happen to do today, which is what makes the guarantee hold
when the bodies change.

## Borrows end when they are last used, not at the end of the block

```rust
let first = &v[0];
println!("{}", first);      // last use of `first`
v.push(99);                 // fine - the shared borrow is already over
```

This compiles. The borrow checker uses **non-lexical lifetimes**: a borrow lasts
from its creation to its last use, not to the closing brace. Before Rust 2018 it
was lexical and this exact code was rejected, which was the single most common
complaint about the language.

Worth knowing because it changes how you write code. You rarely need to
introduce a block scope to end a borrow early; just use the reference and stop.

## Iterating, three ways

```rust
for x in &v          { s += *x; }      // x: &i64     - read
for x in v.iter_mut() { *x += d; }     // x: &mut i64 - write
for x in v           { s += x; }       // x: i64      - CONSUMES v
```

The third one moves the vector into the loop and destroys it - after it, `v` is
gone. That is occasionally what you want and is a surprise the first time it
happens by accident. `&v` and `&mut v` are the forms you want when the container
should survive.

In both of the first two, `x` is a reference, so `*x` is the number. Rust often
auto-dereferences for method calls but not for arithmetic, which is why `s += *x`
needs the star and `x.abs()` would not.

## Why C++ references are not the same thing

```cpp
void add_to_all(std::vector<long long>& v, long long d);   // looks identical
```

A C++ `&` borrows in the same mechanical sense - no copy, writes reach the
original - and carries **no rule at all**. Nothing stops you holding a reference
to an element while another reference reallocates the container, or sharing a
non-const reference across threads. The `const` in `const std::vector<T>&` is
genuinely useful and only covers half of it: it stops *this* code from writing,
not other code from writing while this code reads.

That difference is why `const&` is a convention in C++ and `&` versus `&mut` is
a checked property in Rust. The C++ version is more flexible and the mistakes are
yours to find.

## Overflow, debug and release

Rust's integer arithmetic **panics on overflow in debug builds** and **wraps in
release builds**. Both are defined - neither is undefined behaviour the way
signed overflow is in C++ - but they differ, which means a test suite run in
debug can catch an overflow that production would silently wrap.

That is why this problem keeps values well inside range rather than testing the
boundary: assigning a fixed expected output to an overflowing case would make the
answer depend on which profile compiled it. The explicit, profile-independent
tools are `checked_add` (returns `Option`), `saturating_add` (clamps) and
`wrapping_add` (always wraps) - and reaching for one of those is how you say
which behaviour you actually meant.
